nameStory: The name 'multiflora' means 'many flowers' in Latin, and one look at this rose in bloom explains why! Each branch tip explodes with clusters of dozens of small white flowers, creating spectacular floral displays that can be seen from quite a distance. It's like nature decided to throw confetti across the landscape.
description: Multiflora rose is a vigorous, thorny shrub that forms dense, arching thickets up to 10 feet tall and even wider. This non-native rose was originally planted for erosion control and wildlife habitat but has become aggressively invasive throughout New England. Its long, flexible canes create impenetrable tangles that can swallow up entire fields, roadsides, and forest edges with their sprawling growth.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense clusters of small white flowers (occasionally pink-tinged) bloom in late spring to early summer, each flower about 3/4 inch across with 5 petals and a sweet, honey-like fragrance that attracts bees from far away

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-9 small, oval leaflets that feel smooth on top but slightly fuzzy underneath, with distinctly toothed edges that feel serrated when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Curved, sharp thorns (technically prickles) scattered along the stems that hook backward like cat claws, making it nearly impossible to pull free once you're caught

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long, arching canes that bend over and root where they touch the ground, creating dense, impenetrable thickets that can spread rapidly across large areas

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round red rose hips about 1/4 inch across that persist through winter, often covering the plant in bright red clusters that birds love to eat

idTips.label: Stipules
idTips.description: Fringed, feathery stipules (small leaf-like structures) at the base of each leaf stem that look like tiny green combs - a distinctive feature among roses

habitat: Thrives in disturbed areas, field edges, roadsides, abandoned lots, and forest margins throughout New England from sea level to moderate elevations. Prefers sunny to partially shaded locations with well-drained soils but adapts to almost any conditions. Often found climbing over fences, stone walls, and other vegetation in rural and suburban areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in early spring, followed by spectacular blooms in late May through June that fill the air with sweet fragrance and buzzing bees.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, small green rose hips begin forming while the plant puts energy into extending its long, arching canes that may grow several feet in a season.
seasonality.fall: Rose hips ripen to bright red, creating colorful displays that persist into winter, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny canes remain visible as dense brown tangles, with bright red rose hips often persisting to feed winter birds, and the overall thicket structure becomes most apparent.

funFact: A single multiflora rose plant can produce up to a million seeds per year, and birds that eat the rose hips can spread those seeds up to two miles away in their droppings - which is why you'll often find these roses sprouting in the most unexpected places!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with native swamp rose, but multiflora rose has those distinctive fringed, feathery stipules at the leaf bases (swamp rose has smooth, narrow stipules) and grows in much denser, more aggressive thickets. Remember: fringed stipules = foreign invader!
contextualKnowledge: Originally promoted by government agencies in the mid-1900s as a 'living fence' for farms and wildlife habitat, multiflora rose is now banned or restricted in many states due to its invasive nature. Despite being called a 'problem plant,' it does provide food and shelter for wildlife - it's just too aggressive for its own good.
compareHints: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules. Native roses like Carolina rose and Virginia rose have much simpler flower arrangements and smooth stipules. Rugosa rose has larger, more wrinkled leaves and much bigger flowers, while dog rose has larger individual flowers but fewer per cluster.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
